intro: The New Testament is the second part of the Christian Bible. It is much shorter than the Hebrew Bible, only 27 books, and all of them were written in Greek. The first four books tell the story of Jesus. The rest tell what his followers did and wrote in the years after him.

In this unit you will read about the life of Jesus as the four Gospels tell it: his birth, his teaching in parables, his last week in Jerusalem and, as Christians believe, his rising from the dead. Then you will follow the book of Acts from Jerusalem to Rome, and open a letter that a church in Corinth heard read aloud.

We read these books the way we read any important old text in a public school. We ask what the text says, who wrote it, and how Jewish, Christian and other readers have understood it. By the end you will be able to name the four Gospels, tell a parable, explain what a letter to a church did, and say why Christmas and Easter matter to Christians.
bigQuestion: How does the New Testament tell the story of Jesus and his first followers, and how have its readers understood that story?

timeline.t: Jesus is born, in the years of King Herod, as Matthew and Luke tell it
John the Baptist preaches and baptizes at the Jordan River
Jesus is put to death in Jerusalem at Passover; Christians believe he rose on the third day
Pentecost in Jerusalem; the followers of Jesus begin to spread, as Acts tells it
Saul sees a light on the road to Damascus and becomes a follower
Paul's journeys to Cyprus, Turkey and Greece; churches begin in Philippi, Corinth and Ephesus
1 Thessalonians, which many scholars call the oldest New Testament book
Paul reaches Rome as a prisoner; the book of Acts ends
Rome destroys the Temple in Jerusalem; many scholars date Mark's Gospel about now
Matthew, Luke and John are written; Revelation near the end of this span
Athanasius lists the 27 books of the New Testament

words.d: "good news"; one of the four books, Matthew, Mark, Luke and John, that tell the story of Jesus
the second part of the Christian Bible: 27 books written in Greek
Hebrew for "anointed one"; Christ in Greek. Christians believe Jesus was the messiah; Jewish tradition still waits
a student who follows a teacher; the Gospels name twelve who followed Jesus
a short everyday story with a deeper meaning, like the sower or the Good Samaritan
the long talk in Matthew 5–7, with the Beatitudes and the Golden Rule
rising from the dead; Christians believe Jesus rose on the third day and celebrate it at Easter
"one who is sent"; a leader sent out to tell others about Jesus
the harvest holiday fifty days after Passover; in Acts 2, the day the Holy Spirit came
a person who is not Jewish
a letter; 21 books of the New Testament are letters
Greek for "unveiling"; a kind of writing full of visions and symbols, like Revelation

test.q: Which four books are the Gospels?
test.why: The four Gospels are Matthew, Mark, Luke and John, the first books of the New Testament.

test.q: In what language were the New Testament books written?
test.why: All 27 books were written in Greek, the shared language of the Roman world.

test.q: Which Gospel tells about shepherds visiting the baby Jesus?
test.why: Luke 2 tells of the manger and the shepherds. Matthew tells of the wise men.

test.q: Who baptized Jesus in the Jordan River, according to the Gospels?
test.why: All four Gospels tell of John the Baptist, who baptized people in the Jordan.

choices: a short story with a deeper meaning
test.why: Jesus taught with parables, everyday stories that carry a deeper meaning.

test.q: In the Good Samaritan story, who helps the hurt man?
test.why: The priest and Temple helper pass by. The Samaritan, an outsider, stops to help.

choices: Treat others the way you want to be treated
test.why: Matthew 7:12 in the Sermon on the Mount gives the Golden Rule.

test.q: What do Christians remember at Easter?
test.why: Easter celebrates the resurrection, which Christians believe took place on the third day.

test.q: How do Jewish tradition and Christian belief differ about Jesus?
choices: Christians believe he was the messiah; Jewish tradition does not
test.why: Christians believe Jesus was the messiah. Jewish tradition still waits for the messiah.

test.q: Which book is a sequel to the Gospel of Luke?
test.why: Acts begins by addressing Theophilus, like Luke. Tradition says the same author wrote both.

test.q: What happened to Saul on the road to Damascus?
choices: He saw a bright light and heard a voice
test.why: Acts 9 says a light flashed, Saul fell down and heard a voice saying it was Jesus.

test.q: What did Paul do in each new city, according to Acts?
choices: He spoke in the synagogue first
test.why: Paul went first to the Jewish synagogue, then spoke to anyone who would listen.

test.q: Which letter has the chapter about love that says "the greatest of these is charity"?
test.why: 1 Corinthians 13 is the love chapter. The KJV uses "charity" for love.

test.q: What kind of writing is Revelation?
choices: apocalypse, full of visions and symbols
test.why: Revelation is an apocalypse, like Daniel. It uses pictures and numbers to give hope.

test.q: How many books are in the New Testament?
test.why: The New Testament has 27 books: 4 Gospels, Acts, 21 letters and Revelation.

write.prompt: Pick a question: How does Luke show who counts as a neighbor? Or: What did a letter do for a church far from Paul? Use two or three passages from this unit (such as Luke 10:25–37, Luke 15:11–32, Acts 2:1–4, 1 Corinthians 13:1–13). Tell what each passage says and how Christians and other readers have understood it.
tips: Name the book, chapter and verses for each passage you use.
Say who believes what: "Christians believe…" or "many scholars think…", not "we believe."
Compare readings instead of judging which is right.
Use the unit's words: parable, gospel, apostle, epistle.
Keep your sentences short and say one idea at a time.

title: The New Testament Story

chapters.title: The Life of Jesus in the Gospels
chapters.bigQuestion: How do four different books tell the story of one life, and why do Christians read all four?

story.title: The Father Who Ran
story.kicker: A son asks for his money early, wastes it all, and walks home expecting the worst.
paragraphs: Ms. Ortega's class sits in a circle with the reading lights low. "Today's story comes from the Gospel of Luke," she says. "Jesus told it to a crowd. Listen for the moment that surprises you." She opens the book to chapter 15 and begins.

A man had two sons. The younger one said, "Father, give me my share of the money now." The father did. The son packed up, went far away, and spent everything on parties. Then a famine came. He had no food. He took a job feeding pigs, and he was so hungry he wanted to eat what the pigs ate.

Sitting with the pigs, the son thought about home. "My father's workers have plenty of bread," he said. "I will go back. I will say I am sorry. I will ask to be a worker, not a son." He stood up and started the long walk home, practicing his speech.

Ms. Ortega stops. "Here is the part I want you to see." She reads slowly: while the son was still far down the road, his father saw him. The father ran. He hugged his son and kissed him. The son began his speech, but the father was already calling for a robe, a ring and a feast.

Marcus raises his hand. "He didn't even let him finish." Ms. Ortega nods. "Jesus told stories like this one. People have read them for almost two thousand years. This unit is about the book those stories are in."
story.think: The father ran before the son said one word. What do you think the story wants its listeners to notice about the father?

lessons.title: What a Gospel Is
lessons.mainIdea: The New Testament begins with four books called Gospels, and each one tells the story of Jesus in its own way.
reading: Open a New Testament and the first four books are Matthew, Mark, Luke and John. Each one is called a *gospel*. The word comes from an old English word meaning "good news." Christians use it for the story of Jesus. Each Gospel tells that story from beginning to end.

The four books do not copy each other. Mark is the shortest and moves fast. Matthew quotes the Hebrew Bible often. Luke tells the most parables and pays attention to the poor. John is different from the other three. It uses long speeches and calls Jesus "the Word."

Many scholars think Mark was written first, around 70 CE. Matthew and Luke came later and share many of Mark's stories. Christian tradition names the authors as two *disciples* (Matthew and John) and two of their friends (Mark and Luke). The books themselves do not sign their names.

words.d: "good news"; one of the four New Testament books that tell the story of Jesus
a student who follows a teacher; in the Gospels, one of the people who followed Jesus
the second part of the Christian Bible: 27 books about Jesus and his first followers, written in Greek

look.title: How Long Each Gospel Is
look.cite: Chapter counts in the King James Version (1611) and every standard Bible
look.prompt: Which Gospel is the shortest? Which two are closest in length?

check.q: What does the word gospel mean?
check.why: Gospel comes from an old English word for "good news." Christians use it for the story of Jesus.

check.q: Which Gospel do many scholars think was written first?
check.why: Many scholars think Mark came first, around 70 CE, and that Matthew and Luke used it.

check.q: Which Gospel is most different from the other three?
check.why: John uses long speeches and calls Jesus "the Word." Matthew, Mark and Luke share many of the same stories.

lessons.title: Judea Under Rome
lessons.mainIdea: The Gospels take place in a land ruled by Rome, where Jewish people prayed at the Temple and hoped for freedom.
reading: The story of Jesus happens in a small land by the Mediterranean Sea. The Gospels call parts of it *Judea* and *Galilee*. The people there were Jewish. They read the Torah, kept the Sabbath and traveled to the *Temple* in Jerusalem for holidays. Jesus and his first followers were Jewish too.

But the land was not free. The Roman Empire ruled it. Rome collected taxes and sent soldiers. A king named Herod ruled for Rome when Jesus was born. Later a Roman governor named Pontius Pilate ruled Judea. The Gospels mention both men by name.

Many Jewish people hoped for a leader sent by God, called the *messiah*. They did not agree on what that leader would do. Jewish tradition still waits for the messiah. Christians believe Jesus was the messiah. The Greek word for messiah is "Christ." That is where the name "Jesus Christ" comes from.

words.d: the southern part of the land in the Gospels, around Jerusalem; ruled by Rome in Jesus's time
the great house of worship in Jerusalem where Jewish people brought offerings and gathered on holidays
a Hebrew word meaning "anointed one"; a leader many Jewish people hoped God would send. In Greek, "Christ"

look.title: A Coin in Your Hand
look.text: Imagine you live in Galilee in Jesus's time. A tax collector asks for a coin. You look at it. The face on the coin is the Roman emperor, far away in Rome. Your family reads the Torah and prays at the Temple, but your taxes go to Rome. Some neighbors want to fight Rome. Some say wait. Some say pray.
look.prompt: What might it feel like to hold that coin? Why might people hope for a leader sent by God?

check.q: Who ruled the land where the Gospels take place?
check.why: Rome ruled Judea and Galilee in the time of Jesus. Herod and Pilate governed for Rome.

check.q: What does the word messiah mean?
check.why: Messiah is Hebrew for "anointed one." The Greek word is "Christ."

check.q: How do Jewish tradition and Christian belief differ about the messiah?
choices: Both say the messiah was Herod
Christians believe Jesus was the messiah; Jewish tradition still waits
Jewish tradition says Jesus was the messiah; Christians disagree
check.why: Christians believe Jesus was the messiah. Jewish tradition does not, and still hopes for the messiah to come.

lessons.title: Two Birth Stories
lessons.mainIdea: Luke and Matthew each tell the birth of Jesus in Bethlehem, but they tell it with different visitors and different details.
reading: Only two Gospels tell about the birth of Jesus. Luke tells it one way. Mary and Joseph travel to *Bethlehem*. There is no room at the inn. Mary lays her baby in a *manger*, a feeding box for animals. Angels tell shepherds in the fields, and the shepherds hurry to see the child.

Matthew tells it another way. Wise men from the east follow a star. They ask King Herod where the new king is. Herod is afraid and angry. The wise men find the child in Bethlehem and give gold and two sweet-smelling gifts, frankincense and myrrh. Then Joseph takes the family to Egypt to escape Herod.

Mark and John do not tell a birth story at all. Mark begins with Jesus as a grown man. Readers have noticed these differences for a long time. Many Christmas scenes put shepherds and wise men together, but in the Bible they come from two different books.

words.d: a small town near Jerusalem; Luke and Matthew both say Jesus was born there
a box that holds food for animals; in Luke, the baby Jesus's first bed

look.title: Luke's Shepherds
look.text: In Luke's telling, shepherds are watching their sheep at night. An angel appears and says, "Do not be afraid. I bring you good news of great joy for all people. Today in the city of David a Savior is born." Then many angels sing, and the shepherds go to find the baby.
look.cite: Luke 2:8–16, told in simple words from the King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: Why might Luke choose shepherds, ordinary workers, to be the first visitors?

check.q: Which Gospel tells about the shepherds and the manger?
check.why: Luke 2 tells of the manger and the shepherds. Matthew tells of the wise men and the star.

check.q: Which Gospel tells about the wise men and the star?
check.why: Matthew 2 tells of wise men who follow a star and bring gifts to Bethlehem.

check.q: Which two Gospels do not tell a birth story?
check.why: Mark begins with Jesus as an adult, and John begins with "the Word." Only Matthew and Luke tell about the birth.

lessons.title: John at the River
lessons.mainIdea: All four Gospels say a preacher named John the Baptist came before Jesus and baptized people in the Jordan River.
reading: Before Jesus began teaching, the Gospels say a man named John was preaching by the *Jordan River*. He wore rough clothes made of camel hair and ate locusts and wild honey. He told people to turn away from wrong and get ready. Crowds came out from the towns to hear him.

John dipped people in the river as a sign of a fresh start. This is called *baptism*. It is why he is called John the Baptist. Jesus came to the river, and John baptized him. The Gospels say the sky opened and a voice said, "This is my beloved Son."

All four Gospels tell about John. That is rare. He is one of the few people who appear in every Gospel. Today many Christian churches still baptize people with water. Some dip the whole person. Some sprinkle water on the head. They point back to this story.

words.d: dipping or sprinkling with water as a sign of a fresh start; a practice many Christians keep today
the river east of Judea and Galilee where the Gospels say John baptized people

look.title: Two Ways to Baptize
look.text: Church A: A grown man in a white robe walks into a pool. The pastor dips him all the way under and lifts him up. Church B: A baby in a white dress is held over a stone basin. The priest pours a little water on her head three times. Both churches say they are doing what John did at the river.
look.prompt: What is the same in both churches? What is different? Why might each church do it its way?

check.q: What did John do at the Jordan River?
check.why: John dipped people in the river as a sign of a fresh start. That is why he is called John the Baptist.

check.q: How many Gospels tell about John the Baptist?
check.why: John the Baptist appears in Matthew, Mark, Luke and John. Few people appear in all four.

check.q: Why do many churches baptize with water today?
choices: They point back to the story of John and Jesus at the river
check.why: Christians connect baptism to John baptizing Jesus in the Jordan. Churches do it in different ways.

lessons.title: Twelve Followers
lessons.mainIdea: The Gospels say Jesus chose twelve disciples, ordinary workers like fishermen, to travel and learn with him.
reading: The Gospels say Jesus walked by the Sea of Galilee and saw fishermen at work. He called Simon and his brother Andrew, and then James and John. Mark says he told them, "Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men." They left their nets and went with him.

In time there were twelve. They are called the *disciples*, which means students. Simon got a new name, *Peter*, which means "rock." Matthew was a tax collector, a job people disliked. Thomas asked hard questions. Judas is the one who, the Gospels say, later handed Jesus over.

Why twelve? Many readers connect the number to the twelve tribes of Israel from the Hebrew Bible. The Gospels also name women who traveled with Jesus and paid for the group's needs, like Mary Magdalene and Joanna. Luke says this in chapter 8.

words.d: the new name Jesus gave to Simon the fisherman; it means "rock"
a large lake in the north where the Gospels say Jesus called fishermen to follow him

look.title: Fishers of Men
look.text: And Jesus said unto them, Come ye after me, and I will make you to become fishers of men.
look.prompt: The men caught fish for a living. What might "fishers of men" mean in their new job?

check.q: What job did Simon and Andrew have when Jesus called them?
check.why: Mark 1 says they were casting nets into the Sea of Galilee when Jesus called them.

check.q: What does the new name Peter mean?
check.why: Peter comes from the Greek word for rock. Jesus gave this name to Simon.

check.q: Which number in the Hebrew Bible do many readers connect to the twelve disciples?
check.why: Many readers link the twelve disciples to the twelve tribes of Israel, the sons of Jacob.

lessons.title: Stories With a Point
lessons.mainIdea: Jesus taught with short stories called parables, and the parable of the sower shows how they work.
reading: The Gospels say crowds came to hear Jesus teach. He often taught with a *parable*, a short story about everyday life with a deeper meaning. Seeds, sheep, bread, coins and vineyards fill his stories. Listeners knew these things well. The meaning was for them to figure out.

One famous parable is the sower. A farmer scatters seed. Some falls on the path, and birds eat it. Some falls on rocks and dries up. Some falls in weeds and gets choked. Some falls on good soil and grows a huge crop. Matthew, Mark and Luke all tell this story.

Then the disciples ask what it means. Jesus explains that the seed is the message, and the soils are the people who hear it. Some forget. Some give up. Some let worries crowd it out. Some take it in and change. Many teachers still use this parable to talk about listening.

words.d: a short story about everyday life that carries a deeper meaning; Jesus's favorite way to teach
a farmer who scatters seed by hand; the main figure in one of Jesus's best-known parables

look.title: Where Some Parables Appear
look.cite: Matthew 13, Mark 4, Luke 8 (sower); Matthew 13, Mark 4, Luke 13 (mustard seed); Matthew 18, Luke 15 (lost sheep); Luke 10 and Luke 15 (Samaritan, prodigal son)
look.prompt: Which parables appear only in Luke? What does that tell you about Luke's Gospel?

check.q: What is a parable?
choices: a short story with a deeper meaning
check.why: A parable is a short everyday story that carries a deeper meaning. Jesus taught with them often.

check.q: In the parable of the sower, what happens to seed on the path?
check.why: The seed on the path is eaten by birds. The seed on good soil grows a big crop.

check.q: Which Gospels tell the parable of the sower?
check.why: The sower is in Matthew 13, Mark 4 and Luke 8. It is not in John.

lessons.title: A Neighbor and a Lost Son
lessons.mainIdea: Two parables found only in Luke, the Good Samaritan and the prodigal son, are about kindness to someone you did not expect to love.
reading: In Luke 10, a lawyer asks Jesus, "Who is my neighbor?" Jesus answers with a story. A man is beaten by robbers and left on the road. A priest walks by. A Temple helper walks by. Then a *Samaritan* stops. Samaritans and Jews did not get along in those days. The Samaritan bandages the man and pays for his care.

Jesus asks the lawyer, "Which one was a neighbor?" The lawyer says, "The one who showed mercy." Jesus says, "Go and do the same." The story does not define "neighbor" with a rule. It shows a neighbor in action. Today "Good Samaritan" means anyone who helps a stranger.

Luke 15 holds the story you heard at the start of this chapter. A younger son wastes his money and comes home. His father runs to meet him. The older brother is angry and will not come to the party. People call this the parable of the *prodigal* son. Prodigal means wasteful.

words.d: a person from Samaria, a region between Judea and Galilee; Samaritans and Jews were not friendly in Jesus's time
wasteful with money; the name readers gave to the younger son in Luke 15

look.title: Who Was the Neighbor?
look.text: In Luke's telling, Jesus finishes the story and asks which of the three men was a neighbor to the man the robbers hurt. The lawyer answers, "The one who showed mercy on him." Jesus says, "Go, and do the same."
look.cite: Luke 10:36–37, told in simple words from the King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: The lawyer asked "Who is my neighbor?" Jesus asked a different question back. How is it different?

check.q: Who stops to help the hurt man in the parable in Luke 10?
check.why: The priest and the Temple helper pass by. The Samaritan, from a group Jews did not like, stops and helps.

check.q: What does prodigal mean?
check.why: Prodigal means wasteful. The younger son in Luke 15 wasted his share of the money.

check.q: In the parable of the lost son, what does the father do when he sees his son far off?
choices: He calls the older brother first
check.why: Luke 15:20 says the father saw him a long way off, ran, hugged him and kissed him.

lessons.title: Teaching on a Hill
lessons.mainIdea: Matthew gathers many of Jesus's sayings into one long talk on a hill, the Sermon on the Mount, in chapters 5 to 7.
reading: Matthew 5, 6 and 7 hold the longest talk by Jesus in the Gospels. He goes up a hill, sits down, and teaches. Readers call it the *Sermon on the Mount*. Luke has a shorter version, given on flat ground. It begins with short blessings called the *Beatitudes*.

Each blessing names people who are not on top and says they are blessed. Blessed are the poor in spirit. Blessed are those who mourn. Blessed are the meek, the peacemakers, and those who are treated badly for doing right. Christians have memorized these lines for centuries.

The sermon also gives the *Golden Rule*: treat others the way you want to be treated. It teaches a prayer that Christians call the Lord's Prayer. It says to love your enemies and not to show off when you give or pray. Many of these ideas also appear in Jewish teaching of the same time.

words.d: the long talk in Matthew 5–7 where Jesus teaches on a hill
the short blessings that open the Sermon on the Mount: "Blessed are the…"
treat other people the way you want them to treat you; Matthew 7:12

look.title: A Blessing to Read Aloud
look.text: Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God.
look.prompt: What is a peacemaker? Name one thing a peacemaker at school might do.

check.q: Which chapters of Matthew hold the Sermon on the Mount?
check.why: The Sermon on the Mount fills Matthew 5–7. Luke has a shorter sermon on a plain.

check.q: What are the Beatitudes?
choices: a list of the twelve disciples
check.why: The Beatitudes open the sermon. Each one says a group of people is blessed.

check.q: What does the Golden Rule say?
choices: Save your gold for the Temple
Treat others the way you want to be treated
check.why: Matthew 7:12 says to do to others what you would want them to do to you.

lessons.title: Stories of Healing
lessons.mainIdea: The Gospels tell many stories in which Jesus heals sick people, and Christians read them as signs of who he was.
reading: Many stories in the Gospels show Jesus healing. A man who cannot walk is lowered through a roof by his friends, and Jesus tells him to get up. A woman touches the edge of his cloak and is well. A blind man by the road calls out and is given his sight. The Gospels call these acts *miracles*.

The stories share a pattern. Someone is in need. Someone asks, or Jesus notices. Jesus speaks or touches. The person is well. Often Jesus says, "Your faith has made you whole." Sometimes he asks people to keep it quiet, and they tell everyone anyway.

Christians believe these stories show God's power in Jesus. Other readers study them as the Gospel writers' way of showing who they believed Jesus was. In a public school we read what the text says and how people have read it. We do not decide for anyone what really happened.

words.d: in the Gospels, an act of healing or power that the writers present as a sign from God
trust; in the healing stories, Jesus often says a person's faith has made them well

look.title: Through the Roof
look.text: Mark 2 tells this scene. A house is packed with people listening to Jesus. Four friends carry a man on a mat who cannot walk. They cannot get in the door. So they climb to the flat roof, dig through it, and lower the man down on ropes in front of Jesus. Jesus looks up and sees what the friends have done.
look.prompt: What does the story say about the four friends? Why might Mark include them and not just the man on the mat?

check.q: In Mark 2, how do four friends bring a man to Jesus?
choices: They lower him through the roof
They carry him across the lake
They wait outside for three days
check.why: The house was full, so the friends dug through the roof and lowered the man on his mat.

check.q: What do Christians believe the healing stories show?
check.why: Christians read the healings as signs of God's power in Jesus. Other readers study them as the writers' message about him.

check.q: What does this course do with the healing stories?
choices: Reads what the text says and how readers have understood it
check.why: In a public school we study what the Gospels say and how people have read them. We do not decide what anyone must believe.

lessons.title: Palms and a Supper
lessons.mainIdea: The Gospels tell of Jesus riding into Jerusalem to cheering crowds and sharing a last Passover meal with his disciples.
reading: All four Gospels slow down for the last week. Jesus comes to *Jerusalem* for *Passover*, the holiday that remembers the Exodus from Egypt. He rides in on a young donkey. Crowds wave palm branches and shout "Hosanna!" Christians remember this day as Palm Sunday.

During the week Jesus teaches in the Temple courts and argues with leaders there. Some leaders decide he is dangerous. Judas, one of the twelve, agrees to help them arrest him. The Gospels say he was paid thirty pieces of silver.

On the night before his arrest, Jesus eats a meal with his disciples. Matthew, Mark and Luke say it is the Passover meal. He breaks bread and passes a cup and tells them to remember him. Christians call this the *Last Supper*. Many churches repeat it in a practice called communion or the Eucharist.

words.d: the Jewish holiday that remembers the Exodus from Egypt; the Gospels set the last week of Jesus at Passover
the final meal Jesus shared with his disciples the night before his arrest
the city of the Temple; where the Gospels place the last week of Jesus

look.title: One Meal, Two Holidays
look.text: At a Passover seder, a Jewish family tells the Exodus story with matzah, bitter herbs and four cups of wine. At a church communion, Christians share a small piece of bread and a sip of wine or juice and remember the Last Supper. The Gospels say the Last Supper was a Passover meal in Jerusalem.
look.prompt: How are the two practices alike? How are they different? What does each one remember?

check.q: What holiday brought Jesus to Jerusalem in the last week?
check.why: The Gospels set the last week at Passover, the holiday remembering the Exodus.

check.q: What did the crowds wave when Jesus rode into the city?
check.why: The crowds waved palm branches and shouted "Hosanna." Christians call the day Palm Sunday.

check.q: Which church practice repeats the Last Supper?
check.why: Many churches share bread and wine to remember the Last Supper. They call it communion or the Eucharist.

lessons.title: The Cross and the Empty Tomb
lessons.mainIdea: The Gospels say Jesus was put to death on a cross by Rome and, as Christians believe, rose from the dead on the third day.
reading: After the supper, the Gospels say Jesus prays in a garden and is arrested. He is questioned by Jewish leaders and then by Pilate, the Roman governor. Pilate orders him put to death on a *cross*. This was a Roman punishment. The event is called the *crucifixion*. Christians remember it on Good Friday.

Jesus dies on a Friday and is buried in a tomb cut from rock. A stone is rolled across the door. On Sunday morning, women who followed him come to the tomb. The stone is moved. The tomb is empty. All four Gospels say Mary Magdalene was there.

The Gospels say Jesus rose from the dead and met his followers. Christians call this the *resurrection* and celebrate it at Easter. It is the center of Christian belief. Jewish tradition does not share this belief. Historians can study the texts, but they cannot prove or disprove what happened in the tomb.

words.d: death on a cross, a Roman punishment; the Gospels say Jesus died this way
rising from the dead; Christians believe Jesus rose on the third day and celebrate it at Easter
Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor of Judea who the Gospels say ordered the crucifixion

look.title: At the Tomb
look.text: In Matthew's telling, the women arrive at the tomb on the first day of the week. An angel tells them not to be afraid. "He is not here," the angel says, "for he is risen, as he said. Come, see the place where he lay."
look.cite: Matthew 28:5–6, told in simple words from the King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: Who are the first people to hear this news in Matthew? Why might that matter to readers?

check.q: Who ordered the crucifixion, according to the Gospels?
check.why: The Gospels say Pontius Pilate, ruling Judea for Rome, gave the order. The cross was a Roman punishment.

check.q: What do Christians celebrate at Easter?
check.why: Easter celebrates the resurrection, which Christians believe happened on the third day.

check.q: Which person do all four Gospels place at the empty tomb?
check.why: Every Gospel names Mary Magdalene among those who came to the tomb on Sunday morning.

review.q: How many Gospels are in the New Testament?
review.why: Matthew, Mark, Luke and John are the four Gospels.

review.q: Which empire ruled Judea in the time of Jesus?
review.why: Rome ruled the land. Herod and then Pilate governed for Rome.

review.q: The Greek word for messiah is:
review.why: Messiah (Hebrew) and Christ (Greek) both mean "anointed one."

review.q: Which Gospel tells about the wise men?
review.why: Matthew 2 tells of wise men following a star. Luke tells of shepherds.

review.q: Which parable is found only in Luke?
review.why: The Good Samaritan is in Luke 10 only. The sower and mustard seed are in three Gospels.

review.q: Where is the Sermon on the Mount found?
review.why: Matthew gathers the sayings of Jesus into chapters 5, 6 and 7.

review.q: What happened at the Last Supper?
choices: Jesus told the parable of the sower
Jesus shared bread and a cup and said to remember him
review.why: At the Last Supper Jesus broke bread and passed a cup. Many churches repeat this in communion.

review.q: How does this course treat the resurrection story?
choices: It describes what the Gospels say and what Christians believe
It says the story is false
review.why: In a public school we describe the text and how Christians read it. We do not tell anyone what to believe.

chapters.title: Acts, Paul's Letters and the Early Church
chapters.bigQuestion: How did a small group of followers in Jerusalem grow into churches around the sea, and what did they write to each other?

story.title: A Letter Comes to Corinth
story.kicker: A messenger steps off a ship with a scroll, and a whole church crowds into one house to hear it.
paragraphs: Corinth is a busy port city in Greece. Ships come and go all day. It is around the year 55 CE. A traveler walks up from the harbor with a rolled-up scroll under his arm. He is looking for a house where a group of Christians meets. He has a letter from Paul.

Word spreads fast. By evening the house is full. Men and women, rich and poor, free people and slaves sit close together. Some were born Jewish. Many were not. They all remember Paul. He lived in Corinth for a year and a half and helped start their group. Now he is far away in Ephesus.

The letter is long. It is written in Greek on papyrus. A reader unrolls it and begins: "Paul, called to be an apostle… to the church of God at Corinth." People lean in. Paul has heard about their fights. He has heard that some think they are better than others. He is not happy.

Then the reader gets to a part that makes the room go quiet. Paul writes about love. Love is patient. Love is kind. Love does not brag. Love does not give up. Someone asks the reader to go back and read it again.

That letter is now called 1 Corinthians. It is in every New Testament. This chapter is about how the followers of Jesus spread from Jerusalem to cities like Corinth, and about the letters they left behind.
story.think: Why might a letter matter so much to a group that met in one house? What can a letter do that a visit cannot?

lessons.title: Luke's Second Book
lessons.mainIdea: The Acts of the Apostles picks up where the Gospel of Luke ends and tells how the followers of Jesus spread out from Jerusalem.
reading: Right after the four Gospels comes a book called the *Acts of the Apostles*, or just Acts. It is a sequel. It begins by speaking to the same person Luke's Gospel speaks to, a man named Theophilus. Christian tradition says Luke wrote both books. Many scholars agree they have one author.

The word *apostle* means "one who is sent." Acts follows the people Jesus sent out. In chapter 1, Jesus tells them they will be witnesses in Jerusalem, then in Judea and Samaria, and then to the ends of the earth. The rest of the book follows that map, one step at a time.

The first half of Acts is mostly about Peter in Jerusalem. The second half is mostly about Paul, who travels far. The book ends in Rome. Acts is the only book in the New Testament that tells this history. Without it, readers would not know how the churches began.

words.d: the fifth book of the New Testament; it tells how the followers of Jesus spread from Jerusalem to Rome
"one who is sent"; a leader sent out to tell others about Jesus
the person Luke and Acts are addressed to; the name means "friend of God"

look.title: The Map of Acts
look.text: In Acts 1, before he leaves them, Jesus tells his followers they will be his witnesses in Jerusalem, in all Judea, in Samaria, and to the farthest parts of the earth.
look.cite: Acts 1:8, told in simple words from the King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: Put the four places in order from closest to farthest. How does that order match the way the book of Acts unfolds?

check.q: Which Gospel is Acts a sequel to?
check.why: Acts begins by addressing Theophilus, just as Luke does. Tradition says Luke wrote both.

check.q: What does apostle mean?
check.why: Apostle comes from a Greek word for someone sent out with a message.

check.q: Where does the book of Acts end?
check.why: Acts starts in Jerusalem and ends with Paul in Rome, the capital of the empire.

lessons.title: Wind and Fire at Pentecost
lessons.mainIdea: Acts 2 says that on the holiday of Pentecost the followers of Jesus spoke in many languages, and thousands joined them that day.
reading: Acts 2 opens on *Pentecost*. This is a Jewish harvest holiday fifty days after Passover. In Hebrew it is called Shavuot. Jewish people from many lands had come to Jerusalem for it. The followers of Jesus, about 120 people, were together in one place.

The text says a sound like a strong wind filled the house. Something like small flames rested on each person. Then they began to speak in other languages. Visitors from Egypt, Rome, Arabia and other places each heard their own language. Some laughed and said the speakers must be drunk.

Peter stood up and gave a speech. Acts says about three thousand people joined the group that day. Christians call this the coming of the *Holy Spirit*. Many churches celebrate Pentecost each spring. Some call it the birthday of the church.

words.d: a Jewish harvest holiday fifty days after Passover (Shavuot); in Acts 2, the day the Holy Spirit came
in Christian belief, God's presence and power at work in people; Acts 2 says it came like wind and fire

look.title: Every Language in the Crowd
look.text: Acts 2 lists where the visitors came from: Parthia, Media, Mesopotamia, Judea, Cappadocia, Pontus, Asia, Phrygia, Pamphylia, Egypt, Libya, Rome, Crete and Arabia. Each person heard the message in the language of home. Think about your own school. Count how many languages are spoken in it.
look.prompt: Why might Luke list so many places? What is the story saying about who the message is for?

check.q: How long after Passover is Pentecost?
check.why: Pentecost means "fiftieth." It is the harvest holiday Shavuot, fifty days after Passover.

check.q: What did the visitors hear in Acts 2?
choices: the message in their own languages
check.why: Acts says each visitor heard the followers speaking in the listener's own language.

check.q: Who gave the speech in Acts 2?
check.why: Peter stood up and spoke to the crowd. Acts says about three thousand joined that day.

lessons.title: The First Followers Share
lessons.mainIdea: Acts says the first followers in Jerusalem shared their food and money, while Peter healed and preached at the Temple.
reading: Acts 2 and 4 describe the first group in Jerusalem. They met in homes and at the Temple. They ate together. They shared what they had, so that no one in the group was in need. Some sold land and gave the money to the leaders to hand out. They called each other brothers and sisters.

Peter became the main leader. Acts 3 says he met a man at the Temple gate who could not walk. Peter said, "I have no silver or gold, but what I have I give you," and the man got up. The Temple leaders were not pleased. They arrested Peter more than once and told him to stop.

The group did not yet have a name. Acts 11 says people in Antioch were the first to call them *Christians*. Most of the first followers were Jewish. They kept going to the Temple. A big question was coming: could people who were not Jewish join too?

words.d: a follower of Jesus Christ; Acts 11 says the name was first used in the city of Antioch
a large city in Syria where an early church grew and where Paul's journeys began

look.title: All Things in Common
look.text: Acts describes the first believers this way: they were together, they shared everything they owned, and they sold their goods and gave to anyone who had a need. They met daily at the Temple and broke bread in their homes with glad hearts.
look.cite: Acts 2:44–46, told in simple words from the King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: What would be hard about living this way? What would be good about it?

check.q: How did the first followers in Jerusalem handle their food and money?
choices: They gave it all to Rome
They shared so no one was in need
check.why: Acts 2 and 4 say the group shared what they had, and some sold land to help others.

check.q: Where were followers first called Christians?
check.why: Acts 11:26 says the name Christian was first used in Antioch.

check.q: Who was the main leader of the group in Jerusalem?
check.why: The first half of Acts follows Peter, who preached and healed at the Temple.

lessons.title: A Light on the Road
lessons.mainIdea: Acts 9 tells how Saul, who was chasing the followers of Jesus, became Paul, their most traveled leader.
reading: Acts introduces a man named *Saul*. He was Jewish, from the city of Tarsus, and very serious about the Torah. He believed the followers of Jesus were wrong and dangerous. Acts 8 says he went from house to house to arrest them. He set out for *Damascus* to find more.

Acts 9 says that on the road, a bright light flashed around him. He fell down and heard a voice: "Saul, Saul, why are you hurting me?" The voice said it was Jesus. Saul got up and could not see. His friends led him into the city by the hand. After three days a follower named Ananias came and prayed with him, and Saul could see again.

From then on, Saul told people about Jesus. Acts also calls him *Paul*, a Roman name. He used both. This story was so important that Acts tells it three times. Christians read it as a turning point. Paul himself writes about it more briefly in his letters, such as Galatians 1.

words.d: the Jewish name of Paul; Acts says he arrested followers of Jesus before he joined them
a city in Syria; Acts 9 says Saul was on the road there when he saw a bright light
a city in what is now Turkey; the hometown of Paul

look.title: Before and After
look.text: Before: a man riding toward Damascus with letters giving him power to arrest people. He is sure he is right. After: the same man, blind for three days, led by the hand into the city, waiting. Then he is baptized by one of the people he came to arrest.
look.prompt: Pick one word for Saul before and one word for Saul after. What changed, and what stayed the same?

check.q: What was Saul doing before the road to Damascus?
check.why: Acts 8 and 9 say Saul was hunting the followers of Jesus to put them in prison.

check.q: Where was Saul going when he saw the light?
check.why: Acts 9 says Saul was on the road to Damascus in Syria.

check.q: Which name is Paul's Roman name?
check.why: Saul was his Jewish name and Paul his Roman name. Acts uses both.

lessons.title: Paul's Journeys
lessons.mainIdea: Acts follows Paul on long trips by road and sea to cities around the Mediterranean, where he started groups of followers.
reading: Paul did not stay in one place. Acts describes three long trips, usually called Paul's missionary *journeys*. He started from Antioch each time. He walked Roman roads and sailed on cargo ships. He went to the island of Cyprus, then to cities in what is now Turkey and Greece.

In each city Paul went first to the *synagogue*, the Jewish house of prayer, and spoke there. Then he spoke to anyone who would listen. He worked as a tentmaker to pay his way. He started small groups in Philippi, Thessalonica, Corinth and Ephesus. Some cities welcomed him. In others he was beaten or jailed.

On his last trip in Acts, Paul is a prisoner on a ship to Rome. A storm wrecks the ship near the island of Malta. Everyone swims to shore. Acts 28 ends with Paul in Rome, under guard, still teaching anyone who visits. The book does not say what happened to him after that.

words.d: a long trip; Acts describes three of Paul's trips to start churches, plus his voyage to Rome
a Jewish house of prayer and study; Paul spoke in the synagogue first in each new city

look.title: Stops on Paul's Road
look.cite: Acts of the Apostles, chapters 13–28, King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: Find each city on a map of the Mediterranean. Which way did Paul move over time, east or west?

check.q: What city did Paul start from on his journeys?
check.why: Acts says each journey began at Antioch in Syria.

check.q: Where did Paul usually speak first in a new city?
check.why: Paul went to the Jewish synagogue first, then spoke to anyone who would listen.

check.q: What happened near the island of Malta?
choices: Paul's ship was wrecked in a storm
check.why: Acts 27 tells of the storm and shipwreck near Malta on the way to Rome.

lessons.title: A Meeting in Jerusalem
lessons.mainIdea: Acts 15 tells of a meeting where the leaders decided that people who were not Jewish could join without keeping every law of the Torah.
reading: Most of the first followers were Jewish. But Paul's new groups were full of *Gentiles*, people who were not Jewish. That raised a hard question. Did Gentiles who joined have to keep the laws of the Torah, like the food rules and circumcision? Some leaders said yes. Paul said no.

Acts 15 says the leaders met in Jerusalem to decide. Peter spoke. Paul spoke. James, called the brother of Jesus, led the meeting. In the end they agreed. Gentiles could join without keeping every law. They asked only a few things, such as not eating food offered to idols.

This meeting changed history. It let the movement grow among people of every background. Jewish followers still kept the Torah. Over the next centuries the two groups grew apart. Judaism and Christianity became two separate religions, each with its own reading of the Hebrew Bible.

words.d: a person who is not Jewish; the New Testament uses the word for the many peoples of the Roman world
called the brother of Jesus; Acts 15 shows him leading the meeting in Jerusalem

look.title: Two Sides of a Question
look.text: Side one: "The Torah is God's teaching. Anyone who joins us should keep it all, as we do." Side two: "God welcomed these Gentiles already. Why put a heavy load on them?" Both sides in Acts 15 were Jewish. Both loved the Torah. They still disagreed.
look.prompt: Restate each side in your own words. What did the meeting decide, and what did it still ask of Gentiles?

check.q: What is a Gentile?
choices: a person who is not Jewish
check.why: Gentile means a person who is not Jewish. Paul's new groups had many Gentiles.

check.q: What did the meeting in Acts 15 decide?
choices: Gentiles could not join at all
Gentiles could join without keeping every Torah law
Everyone had to move to Jerusalem
check.why: The leaders agreed Gentiles could join with only a few requests, not the whole law.

check.q: Who led the meeting in Jerusalem?
choices: James, called the brother of Jesus
check.why: Acts 15 shows James giving the final word at the meeting.

lessons.title: What a Letter Can Do
lessons.mainIdea: Twenty-one books of the New Testament are letters, and a letter let a leader teach a church he could not visit.
reading: Paul could not be everywhere. So he wrote letters. A letter in the New Testament is also called an *epistle*. Thirteen letters carry Paul's name. Some scholars think a few of them were written later by his students in his name, which was common then. The letters are named for the people they went to, like Romans and Galatians.

Ancient letters followed a pattern. First the greeting: who is writing, to whom, and a blessing. Then thanks. Then the main part, with teaching and advice. Then the goodbye, with greetings to friends by name. Paul often had a helper write while he spoke, and then signed the end himself.

The letters answer real problems. The Corinthians were fighting. The Galatians were confused about the Torah. The Philippians had sent Paul a gift. Reading a letter is like hearing one side of a phone call. You have to guess what the other side said. Many scholars think 1 Thessalonians is the oldest book in the New Testament, from around 50 CE.

words.d: a letter; the New Testament has 21 of them, 13 with Paul's name
the opening of an ancient letter: who is writing, to whom, and a blessing
a letter from Paul to churches in Galatia, a region in what is now Turkey

look.title: Some of Paul's Letters
look.cite: Chapter counts in the King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: Which letter is the longest? Philemon is one chapter; who do you think it was written to, a big church or one person?

check.q: How many letters in the New Testament carry Paul's name?
check.why: Thirteen letters name Paul as the writer. Some scholars think students wrote a few of them in his name.

check.q: What comes first in an ancient letter?
check.why: Ancient letters began with a greeting: who is writing, to whom, and a blessing.

check.q: Why is reading a letter like hearing one side of a phone call?
choices: We only have the writer's words, not the church's
check.why: We have Paul's answers but not the letters or questions the churches sent him.

lessons.title: The Love Chapter
lessons.mainIdea: In 1 Corinthians 13, Paul tells a fighting church that without love, nothing else they do is worth anything.
reading: The church in *Corinth* had a problem. Some members thought they were better than others. Some had gifts like speaking in other languages or teaching, and they showed off. Paul had heard about it in Ephesus. In chapter 13 of his first letter he changed the subject to love.

He starts big. If I speak every language, even the language of angels, and have no love, I am just a loud noise. If I know everything and have no love, I am nothing. Then he says what love does. Love is patient. Love is kind. It is not jealous. It does not brag. It does not keep a list of wrongs.

He ends with three things that last: faith, hope and love. "The greatest of these is love." The King James Version uses the old word *charity* here instead of love. This chapter is read at many weddings today. But Paul wrote it to a church, to tell them how to treat each other.

words.d: a port city in Greece; Paul started a church there and wrote it at least two letters
the word the King James Version (1611) uses for love in 1 Corinthians 13

look.title: The Greatest of These
look.text: And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity.
look.prompt: "Abideth" means "stays." Charity here means love. Why might Paul put love above faith and hope?

check.q: Why did Paul write about love to the Corinthians?
choices: They had asked for a wedding poem
They wanted to know about Rome
They were fighting and showing off
check.why: 1 Corinthians answers a church that was divided. Chapter 13 tells them love matters more than their gifts.

check.q: What word does the King James Version use for love in this chapter?
check.why: The KJV of 1611 says "charity" where newer translations say "love."

check.q: Which three things does Paul say last?
check.why: 1 Corinthians 13:13 names faith, hope and love, and calls love the greatest.

lessons.title: Letters From Other Leaders
lessons.mainIdea: Besides Paul's letters, the New Testament has letters linked to James, Peter, John and Jude, and one called Hebrews.
reading: Not every letter in the New Testament comes from Paul. Eight more follow his. One is called *Hebrews*. It does not say who wrote it. Tradition once gave it to Paul, but most scholars now say the author is unknown. It compares Jesus to the priests of the Temple.

Then come letters named for their writers instead of their readers. James is full of short, practical advice, like "be quick to listen and slow to speak." Two letters carry Peter's name. Three carry John's name. One short one is from Jude. Because they went to many churches, not just one, they are often called the *general letters*.

These letters show that many leaders, not just Paul, were teaching. They also show the churches facing new problems: false teachers, hard times and long waiting. Scholars discuss who wrote each one and when. The churches kept and copied all of them.

words.d: a New Testament letter with no writer's name; it compares Jesus to the Temple priests
the letters of James, Peter, John and Jude, written to many churches rather than one

look.title: Quick to Listen
look.text: The letter of James tells its readers that everyone should be quick to hear, slow to speak, and slow to get angry.
look.cite: James 1:19, told in simple words from the King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: Which of the three is hardest for you? Why might a letter to a whole church say this?

check.q: Who wrote the letter to the Hebrews?
choices: The letter does not say, and scholars are not sure
check.why: Hebrews names no writer. Tradition once said Paul, but most scholars now say the author is unknown.

check.q: Why are James, Peter, John and Jude called general letters?
choices: They went to many churches, not one
check.why: General letters were sent to many churches instead of to one city like Corinth.

check.q: What advice does James 1 give?
choices: be quick to listen and slow to speak
check.why: James 1:19 says to be quick to hear, slow to speak and slow to anger.

lessons.title: A Book of Pictures
lessons.mainIdea: Revelation, the last book of the Bible, uses strange pictures to give hope to churches in a hard time.
reading: The last book in the New Testament is *Revelation*. Its writer calls himself John and says he is on a small island called Patmos. He writes to seven churches in what is now Turkey. Many scholars think it was written around 95 CE, when the Roman emperor was Domitian and Christians in some places faced trouble.

Revelation is full of pictures. A throne with a rainbow around it. A lamb. A dragon. Four horsemen. A city of gold with gates of pearl. Numbers repeat: seven, twelve, one thousand. This kind of writing is called *apocalypse*, a Greek word meaning "unveiling." The book of Daniel in the Hebrew Bible uses the same style.

Readers have disagreed about Revelation for centuries. Some Christians read it as a map of future events. Others read it as a message to its own time, using code pictures for Rome. Many read its ending as a promise: a new heaven and a new earth, where God wipes away every tear. That promise gives the book its hope.

words.d: the last book of the Bible; a vision written to seven churches, full of symbols and hope
a Greek word meaning "unveiling"; a kind of writing that uses visions and symbols, like Daniel and Revelation
a small island in the Aegean Sea where the writer of Revelation says he was

look.title: No More Tears
look.text: Near the end of Revelation, the writer sees a new heaven and a new earth. A voice says God will live with people and wipe away all tears from their eyes. There will be no more death, no more sorrow, no more crying and no more pain, because the old things have passed away.
look.cite: Revelation 21:1–4, told in simple words from the King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: Why might a church in a hard time want to hear this passage read aloud?

check.q: Where does the writer of Revelation say he is?
check.why: Revelation 1 says John was on Patmos, a small island in the Aegean Sea.

check.q: What does the word apocalypse mean?
check.why: Apocalypse is Greek for "unveiling" or "revealing." It names a kind of writing full of visions.

check.q: How do readers disagree about Revelation?
choices: Everyone agrees it is a history book
Some think Paul wrote it; some think Peter did
Some read it as the future; some read it as a message to its own time
Some say it is in the Torah
check.why: Some Christians read it as future events. Others read its pictures as code for Rome in its own day.

lessons.title: Twenty-Seven Books, Every Land
lessons.mainIdea: The New Testament has 27 books in four kinds, and the faith it describes spread over time to every part of the world.
reading: Now you can see the whole New Testament. It has 27 books. Four are Gospels. One is Acts, the history. Twenty-one are letters. One is Revelation. All were written in Greek, the common language of the Roman world, in the first century or so. Christians read the same 27 books in every church.

The list did not settle all at once. Churches copied and shared the books for a long time. In 367 CE a bishop in Egypt named Athanasius wrote a letter listing exactly these 27. Christians differ about a few books in the Old Testament, but not about the New.

Acts ends in Rome. The story kept going. Over many centuries Christians went to Africa, Asia, Europe and later the Americas. Today there are Christians in nearly every country. Chicago has churches that pray in English, Spanish, Polish, Korean and many more languages, each reading these same books.

words.d: the official list of books in a Bible; the New Testament canon is 27 books
a bishop in Egypt who in 367 CE listed the 27 books of the New Testament

look.title: What Is in the New Testament
look.cite: The 27 books of the New Testament, as listed by Athanasius in 367 CE and in every Christian Bible today
look.prompt: Add up the rows. Which kind of book makes up most of the New Testament?

check.q: How many books are in the New Testament?
check.why: The New Testament has 27 books: 4 Gospels, Acts, 21 letters and Revelation.

check.q: What language were the New Testament books written in?
check.why: The New Testament was written in Greek, the common language of the Roman world.

check.q: What did Athanasius do in 367 CE?
choices: listed the 27 books of the New Testament
check.why: Athanasius, a bishop in Egypt, wrote a letter listing the 27 books Christians still use.

review.q: Which book tells how the followers of Jesus spread from Jerusalem to Rome?
review.why: The Acts of the Apostles tells this history. It is the only New Testament book that does.

review.q: What happened on Pentecost in Acts 2?
choices: The followers spoke in many languages and thousands joined
review.why: Acts 2 tells of wind, fire and many languages. Peter spoke and about three thousand joined.

review.q: What was Saul doing before he became a follower of Jesus?
review.why: Acts 9 says Saul was on his way to Damascus to arrest followers when he saw the light.

review.q: Where did Paul usually speak first in a new city?
review.why: Paul began at the Jewish synagogue in each city, then spoke to others.

review.q: What did the meeting in Acts 15 decide about Gentiles?
choices: They had to move to Rome
They could join without keeping every Torah law
review.why: The Jerusalem meeting agreed Gentiles could join with only a few requests.
Epistle means letter. The New Testament has 21 of them.

review.q: In 1 Corinthians 13, what does Paul say is the greatest?
review.why: Paul names faith, hope and love and says the greatest is love, or "charity" in the KJV.

review.q: Which book ends the New Testament?
review.why: Revelation, the book of visions written to seven churches, is the last book of the Bible.
